title: Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement

concept.text: Concept synthesis. This innovation would replace the essential functions of a failing organ with a durable artificial system that operates safely with little daily intervention. It would integrate physiological sensing, control, power, materials, and the mechanisms that perform the required organ functions. The intended achievement is sustained clinical replacement over years, with manageable maintenance and treatment burden.

Scope synthesis. The functions that must be replaced depend on the organ and the patient’s remaining physiological capacity. Automating insulin delivery addresses part of pancreatic endocrine function. Broader replacement would require a defined account of which essential functions the system supplies and which remain dependent on the patient or additional treatment. Autonomy concerns the system’s ability to respond appropriately during ordinary use and disturbances. Durability concerns continued function and safety over prolonged use. Neither requires perfect control or indefinite operation.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis. A compact, reliable artificial organ could substantially reduce the recurring treatment and daily management required by major organ failure. If it maintained adequate physiological function with fewer interventions, its direct benefits could include reduced treatment burden and greater freedom in everyday life. Those benefits would need to be demonstrated alongside safety and patient outcomes.

Conditional downstream synthesis. Reduced dependence on donor organs would additionally require a device that can clinically substitute for transplantation in an identifiable patient population. Durability, practical maintenance, and acceptable outcomes would determine how widely that substitution could occur. Success in an artificial kidney would establish an organ-specific advance. Claims extending that success to artificial livers, hearts, or a general replacement platform would require additional evidence because their physiological functions and engineering demands differ.

missing_breakthrough.text: Engineering synthesis. The missing capability is reliable integration of organ-function replacement with long-term sensing, control, power, and biological compatibility. A system must deliver enough of the relevant physiological functions across changing patient needs while maintaining safe operation. Requirements depend on the organ, the device architecture, and the amount of residual native function.

Barrier synthesis. The proposed system must address clotting where blood-contacting components create that risk, infection, material degradation, device failure, and harmful control errors over prolonged use. Sensors must remain sufficiently reliable for clinical decisions, control must respond safely to changing physiology, and power and maintenance arrangements must support the intended operating life. These are design requirements inferred from the concept. The supplied evidence does not document their resolution or establish a single architecture applicable to every organ.

Integration synthesis. Improvements in individual components must translate into a dependable complete system. Sensor errors can affect control decisions, device deterioration can alter physiological performance, and maintenance requirements can erode the intended reduction in treatment burden. Convincing progress therefore requires evaluating how components behave together during routine operation, disturbances, and recoverable failures.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Sue A. Brown and colleagues’ Six-Month Randomized, Multicenter Trial of Closed-Loop Control in Type 1 Diabetes, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1907863, and reports an online publication date of 16 October 2019. It describes a six-month randomized comparison in which closed-loop insulin delivery increased time in the target glucose range relative to a sensor-augmented pump. The source index contains the citation but no captured article, abstract, or retained artifact. Consequently, the reported benefit, publication details, and supplied abstract locator remain unverified within this record. The evidence limitation leaves the finding unresolved here and does not establish that it is false.

Interpretive synthesis. The cited trial is intended as a historical example of partial pancreatic endocrine automation. Its described scope concerns glucose control over six months. Establishing durable autonomous organ replacement would additionally require evidence about the essential functions being replaced, prolonged safety and reliability, maintenance, and patient burden. The supplied description provides no basis for inferring multiyear implantability or replacement of other pancreatic functions.

Coverage limitation. This single historical example provides limited coverage of artificial-organ development. The supplied review contains no freshness evidence establishing developments through 1 November 2026. It therefore leaves the present extent of progress across artificial kidneys, hearts, livers, and other organ systems unassessed. The final record cannot establish whether particular contemporary systems meet parts of the proposed goal.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. In a defined major organ-failure condition, comparative clinical trials would demonstrate years of safe, effective replacement with substantially lower treatment burden and acceptable patient outcomes. The evaluation would specify the patient population, essential functions supplied, residual native function, additional treatments, comparator, and follow-up duration. Organ-specific effectiveness, safety, burden, and outcome thresholds would be set before evaluation. These are proposed criteria, and the supplied record does not establish a published consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Trials show years of safe, effective replacement substantially reducing burden

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and reliability evidence. Convincing results would include reproducible performance across patients and clinical settings, together with reported device failures, harmful control events, infections, clotting where relevant, maintenance, and replacement procedures. Follow-up would distinguish sustained device performance from outcomes maintained through frequent rescue treatment or substantial additional patient effort. Safe responses to foreseeable faults and changes in physiological demand would form part of the demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible clinical performance includes reported failures and safe fault responses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries. A successful claim would state the demonstrated operating lifetime, supported patient population, maintenance needs, and circumstances requiring clinical intervention. Perfect control and indefinite operation are unnecessary. A general-platform claim would require successful validation in additional organs. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within their tested populations, durations, and conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Claims state demonstrated operating limits and conditions requiring clinical intervention

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. BME-01, Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand, BME-06, Long-term banking of transplantable human organs, and BME-12, Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation, share the goal of making organ replacement more available. Their titles concern obtaining, preserving, or supplying biological grafts. BME-13 concerns sustained artificial replacement of physiological function. Their potential effects on donor dependence overlap, while each requires its own evidence of clinical suitability.

Roster-based synthesis. BME-11, Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body, and BME-17, Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body, overlap with restoring organ function through tissue-based approaches. BME-13 centers on an artificial replacement system. Hybrid devices could involve both tissue and engineered components, with the classification depending on which capability the claimed advance establishes.

Roster-based synthesis. BME-18, Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers, could provide physiological measurements for autonomous control. BME-16, Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants, overlaps with prolonged compatibility and stable connections to the body. BME-04, A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation, shares challenges involving durable interfaces and feedback. Success in these component or interface capabilities would still leave the organ-specific replacement mechanism and complete-system performance to be demonstrated.

Roster-based synthesis. BME-05, Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body, shares the sense-and-respond principle, implemented through a living therapeutic system. Such medicines could complement artificial-organ control or supply particular functions. BME-08, Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance, could intersect with replacement systems that contain biological components for which immune compatibility matters. The degree of overlap depends on the replacement architecture.

Roster-based synthesis. BME-09, Physiological extra-uterine support through extreme prematurity, and BME-14, Shelf-stable, broadly compatible replacement for critical blood functions, overlap with engineered support or replacement of essential physiology. Their supplied titles define different developmental settings, functions, and practical boundaries. BME-10, Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use, could support design or evaluation of replacement control, while clinical evidence would remain necessary to demonstrate actual long-term replacement.

unresolved_issues: The cited trial’s identity, publication details, reported benefit, and abstract locator remain unverified from retained source content. Obtaining that content could resolve these questions.
The supplied materials do not establish contemporary progress across artificial-organ systems or freshness through 1 November 2026.
The target organ, patient population, device architecture, required functions, and acceptable residual dependence on other treatment remain unspecified.
Organ-specific effectiveness, safety, treatment-burden, comparator, follow-up, and maintenance thresholds remain to be defined for a concrete evaluation.
The supplied evidence does not establish which integration barriers have been resolved in particular systems or whether any system meets the proposed multiyear completion criteria.

brief.title: Artificial organs that work for years with little upkeep
possible: People with organ failure could spend less of everyday life managing treatment. An artificial replacement would supply the failing organ’s essential functions for years, adjust to changing needs and require little daily attention.
why: Reliable replacement could give patients more freedom by reducing recurring treatment and daily management. Devices that could substitute for a transplant would also reduce dependence on donor organs.

sources.showed: This randomized clinical trial compared insulin delivery that adjusts automatically with a pump supported by a glucose sensor.
sources.cited_for: The trial addresses automation of part of the pancreas’s role in controlling blood sugar.
sources.not_established: It does not establish replacement of other pancreatic functions or reliable operation over years.

sources.who: M.R. Mehra and the MOMENTUM 3 Investigators
sources.showed: A heart-assist pump with moving parts suspended by magnets outperformed an older pump. More patients survived without disabling stroke or surgery for device malfunction.
sources.quote:
The numbers of events 
per patient-year for stroke of any severity, major bleeding, and gastrointestinal 
hemorrhage were lower in the centrifugal-flow pump group than in the axial-flow 
pump group.
sources.cited_for: The trial demonstrates improved durability and safety of mechanical heart support.
sources.not_established: Assisting the heart does not establish complete replacement with little daily management.

sources.who: Victor Gura, Matthew B. Rivara and colleagues
sources.showed: A wearable kidney device removed fluid as prescribed without serious adverse events during the study. Its bubble detector stopped the pump, but staff had to remove the bubbles.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates fluid removal and an automatic response to a potentially unsafe condition.
sources.not_established: It does not establish sustained replacement over years or operation with little intervention.

sources.showed: An artificial heart that adjusts pumping to sensed pressure supported a patient until transplantation. This was a single-patient report.
sources.quote: The patient was successfully bridged to transplant after 5 months of support on the device and has made a full recovery.
sources.cited_for: The report demonstrates heart replacement with automatic adjustment outside the hospital.
sources.not_established: A single case ending in transplantation does not establish reliable replacement over years across patients.

shown: Mehra and colleagues demonstrated better outcomes with a magnetically suspended heart-assist pump over 2 years. Their comparison provides evidence of durable support and fewer device complications.
Schroder and colleagues reported an automatically adjusting artificial heart that supported a patient for 5 months before transplantation, including time at home.
missing: A complete replacement must combine reliable sensing, automatic adjustment, power and materials that remain safe in the body.
Comparative trials must establish years of effective replacement with substantially less treatment burden and acceptable patient outcomes.
Performance across patients and settings must include safe fault responses, practical maintenance and transparent reporting of failures.

milestones.label: Trials demonstrate years of safe replacement with less burden
milestones.explanation: Comparative trials would have to show years of safe, effective replacement and substantially less treatment burden in a defined patient group. This would establish lasting clinical benefit.

milestones.label: Clinical results repeat, with failures and safe responses reported
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across patients and settings, with failures, maintenance and safe fault responses reported. This would distinguish dependable operation from outcomes sustained by frequent rescue treatment.

milestones.label: Claims specify operating limits and when clinical help is needed
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to state demonstrated lifetime, eligible patients, upkeep and when clinical intervention is needed. These boundaries would define dependable use; claims spanning organs would require validation in additional organs.

uncertain: Which essential functions must a device supply, and how much remaining organ function or additional treatment is acceptable?
What safety, effectiveness, maintenance and treatment-burden thresholds should each organ replacement meet?
Success with one organ would leave open whether the same approach could work for organs with different functions.

page.title: Autonomous artificial-organ replacement
page.definition: Artificial systems supply biventricular cardiac pumping, kidney clearance and fluid regulation, or pancreatic glucose regulation for years during home use. They adjust output automatically to physiological changes; the pancreatic case concerns glucose control rather than digestive function.

goal.need: During 2024, 167,230 unique patients appeared on United States solid-organ transplant waiting lists, and 70,600 were added. Donor transplantation and recurring replacement treatment present different constraints: the Kidney Health Initiative identifies reduced maintenance and interventions as design goals for implantable kidney replacement.

figures.caption: United States transplant activity reported for 2024
figures.note: Waiting-list figures cover registrations present during the year, including registrations at multiple centres. These are not paired cohorts or year-end counts of unique patients.

statements.context: A patient-centred characteristic specified for implantable kidney replacement in the technology roadmap.

statements.body: United States Food and Drug Administration
statements.quote: where the system can automatically adjust basal insulin and provide insulin for meals.
statements.context: FDA's description of a fully closed-loop insulin-only artificial pancreas.

completion.title: An artificial-organ system gains authorization after 24 months of autonomous home replacement.
completion.criterion: For an organ case, an integrated system meets its registered efficacy and safety endpoints through at least 24 months of home use, adjusts output automatically without routine manual therapy adjustments, and obtains marketing authorization for that replacement indication. Maintenance and rescue treatment remain within the tested protocol. Humanitarian approval based only on probable benefit does not qualify. The 24-month minimum is Atlas-defined, not a regulatory or consensus threshold.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a composite test because no shared cross-organ completion criterion was found.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA device and artificial-pancreas guidance, NHLBI material, the KHI roadmap, KidneyX rules and the published scope of ISO 14708-5 found no shared multiyear autonomy or maintenance test. This composite combines the organ-specific goals; 24 months is the Atlas's minimum interpretation of years. Marketing authorization alone does not establish autonomous operation or two-year performance.

milestones.title: An artificial-organ system passes nonclinical evaluation and receives authorization for first human use.
milestones.criterion: An integrated system completes the nonclinical evaluation accepted for its first significant-risk human study, and FDA and the institutional review board authorize that study. Tests depend on the device and intended use. For AbioCor, the animal protocol required at least 5 calves weighing 90–120 kg, supported for 30 days without thromboembolic complications or tissue injury from transcutaneous energy transfer; 14 completed. Those numerical requirements concern that artificial-heart protocol only.
milestones.set_by: FDA, IDE Approval Process and early-feasibility guidance. The numerical animal-study requirements were specified in the AbioCor protocol reviewed under H040006; they are not cross-organ requirements.
milestones.threshold_quote: Studies of devices that pose a significant risk require both FDA and an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval prior to initiation of a clinical study.

milestones.title: An artificial-organ system demonstrates its intended physiological function in an authorized human study.
milestones.criterion: An authorized feasibility study demonstrates its intended physiological function and initial clinical safety under its protocol. Gura et al. (2 June 2016) enrolled 7 wearable-kidney recipients; 5 completed 24 hours, with no serious adverse events, but technical problems stopped the study and staff removed bubbles. Schroder et al. (21 September 2022) reported one autoregulated-heart recipient supported to transplantation after 5 months and discharged home on postoperative day 75. These are assisted or temporary demonstrations.
milestones.set_by: FDA, early-feasibility guidance issued on 1 October 2013. Functional endpoints, exposure and safety assessments are device-specific; FDA specifies no common numerical clinical-success threshold for these organs.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies may be used to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: An artificial-organ system meets its pivotal protocol's safety and efficacy criteria for home replacement.
milestones.criterion: The final system meets its pivotal protocol's efficacy and safety decision rules for the intended population, home use and replacement claim. Brown et al. (2019): 168 participants, 6 months, glucose time at 70–180 mg/dL improved by 11 percentage points versus control (95% CI 9–14). Mehra et al. (2019): 1,028 LVAD recipients, 76.9% versus 64.8% survived 2 years without disabling stroke or reoperation for device malfunction. These concern glucose regulation and ventricular assistance, respectively; neither establishes the completion test.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Design Considerations for Pivotal Clinical Investigations for Medical Devices, issued on 7 November 2013. Numerical decision rules belong to individual protocols, not to a cross-organ standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: Claims can be supported statistically by formal hypothesis testing or by point estimates with corresponding confidence intervals.

not_found: No shared numerical thresholds for autonomous operating life, maintenance burden or pivotal clinical success were found across the listed organ functions.
The full requirements of ISO 14708-5:2020 were not retrieved; FDA's recognition record supplies its scope.
ClinicalTrials.gov records NCT04117295 and NCT02232659 opened without their study fields, and their API records could not be retrieved.
The full text of the kidney-replacement roadmap published on 6 November 2026 could not be opened.

results.finding: In 1,028 patients, 76.9% assigned the centrifugal-flow LVAD met the 2-year primary endpoint.
results.detail: The trial met its primary endpoint, but the device provides left ventricular assistance rather than biventricular replacement. Patients expected to need biventricular support were excluded.
results.quote:
In the analysis of the 
primary end point, a larger percentage of patients 
in the centrifugal-flow pump group than in the 
axial-flow pump group remained alive and free 
of disabling stroke or reoperation to replace or 
remove a malfunctioning device at 2 years (397 
patients [76.9%] vs. 332 patients [64.8%]).

results.finding: In an FDA-approved wearable-kidney trial, 5 of 7 enrolled subjects completed 24 hours of treatment.
results.detail: The device achieved solute clearance and fluid homeostasis with no serious adverse events. Technical problems stopped the trial, and investigators manually removed bubbles.
results.quote: Of 7 enrolled subjects, 5 completed the planned 24 hours of study treatment. The trial was stopped after the seventh subject due to device-related technical problems, including excessive carbon dioxide bubbles in the dialysate circuit and variable blood and dialysate flows.

results.finding: One Aeson artificial-heart recipient was supported for 5 months before transplantation.
results.detail: The patient was discharged home on postoperative day 75. The report’s comment section states 8 months of support, conflicting with the 5 months stated in the abstract and case description.
results.quote: The patient was successfully bridged to transplant after 5 months of support on the device and has made a full recovery.

results.finding: AbioCor animal study: 14 calves completed 30 days of implanted support.
results.detail: The report describes uncomplicated implant courses and approval of a clinical trial, but does not explicitly state that both FDA and an institutional review board authorized the first human study.
results.quote:
Fourteen calves completed the 30-day implant study duration. Terminations were
elective. The implant courses of these studies were uncomplicated.

results.finding: Closed-loop artificial pancreas trial, sample size not stated: FDA granted an IDE in April 2008.
results.detail: The IDE was based on in silico testing, but the source does not report IRB authorization or establish that this was the system’s first significant-risk human study.
results.quote: Thus the simulator was immediately put to its intended use, and in April 2008, an investigational device exemption (IDE) was granted by the FDA for a closed-loop control clinical trial.

results.finding: Wearable Artificial Kidney: FDA and IRB accepted a US safety-trial protocol for up to 16 patients.
results.detail: The article reports prior human testing abroad and does not establish that the nonclinical evaluation accepted for the first significant-risk human study was completed.
results.quote: The federal Food and Drug Administration and the University of Washington Institutional Review Board accepted the protocol for the clinical trial.

results.finding: AWAK PD: 11 participants entered treatment; all remained within 5% of target weight.
results.detail: The study reported no device-related serious adverse events and achieved ultrafiltration through dextrose adjustment. However, authorization is not stated, and urea and creatinine increased during treatment, leaving solute clearance uncertain.
results.quote: No device-related serious adverse events occurred. 95% of therapies conducted (76/80) were completed. Optimal UF was achieved by adjusting the dextrose concentrations. All subjects remained within 5% of their target weight.

results.finding: In a bihormonal closed-loop trial for type 1 diabetes, 71 participants had a mean glucose time in range of 80.3% at 12 months.
results.detail: The registered, prospective trial assessed performance and safety, but the text does not explicitly establish authorization, identify it as a feasibility study, or conclude that initial clinical safety was demonstrated. Five serious adverse events were reported.
results.quote: After 1 year of FCL treatment, mean TIR was 80·3% (SD 5·4) and median time below range was 1·36% (IQR 0·80-2·11).

results.finding: In 326 participants with type 1 diabetes, the bionic pancreas lowered glycated hemoglobin by an adjusted 0.5 percentage points versus standard care at 13 weeks.
results.detail: The trial also met the prespecified noninferiority margin for time below 54 mg/dL. The text does not establish that the tested device was the final system or that all pivotal safety and efficacy decision rules for the home replacement claim were met.
results.quote: The mean adjusted between-group difference in the glycated hemoglobin level at 13 weeks was −0.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], −0.6 to −0.3; P<0.001).

results.finding: Neokidney pivotal study: 29 participants; 0 serious adverse device effects.
results.detail: These preliminary results cover assisted in-center treatment, not home use. Phase 2 was ongoing, and the abstract does not report the primary efficacy endpoint's confidence interval or final protocol decision.
results.quote: As of August 31st, 2026, 29 participants were included and completed 474 Neokidney sessions (95% of planned Phase 1&2 sessions). No SADEs or device deficiencies with potential to cause a serious adverse event occurred.
